Physics

Motion in One Dimension

Converting with prefixes · SI Base Units and Prefixes1km=1000m,1m=100cm=1000mmkm: kilometre, m: metre, cm: centimetre, mm: millimetre, mg: milligram, g: gram.
Displacement · Distance and Displacement: Scalar vs Vectordisplacement=xf​−xi​xf​: final position, xi​: initial position, in metres. The sign gives direction.
Distance · Distance and Displacement: Scalar vs Vectordistance=sum of all segment lengthsIn metres, never negative.
Average speed · Speed and Velocityaverage speed=total timetotal distance​Distance in metres, time in seconds, so speed is in metres per second.
Average velocity · Speed and Velocityaverage velocity=total timedisplacement​Displacement in metres; the sign of the result gives the direction.
Distance at constant speed · Speed and Velocitydistance=speed×timeDistance in metres, speed in m/s, time in seconds. Hence time =speeddistance​.
Average velocity under constant acceleration · Speed and Velocityaverage velocity=2v0​+v​In m/s; valid only when the acceleration is constant. v0​: initial velocity, v: final velocity.
Velocity from slope · Graphs of Motionv=ΔtΔx​From a position–time graph. Δx in metres, Δt in seconds, v in m/s.
Acceleration from slope · Graphs of Motiona=ΔtΔv​From a velocity–time graph, in m/s2.
Acceleration · Acceleration and the Equations of Motiona=tv−v0​​v: final velocity (m/s), v0​: initial velocity (m/s), t: time (s), a: acceleration (m/s2).
First equation · Acceleration and the Equations of Motionv=v0​+atLinks velocity and time.
Second equation · Acceleration and the Equations of MotionΔx=v0​t+21​at2Δx: displacement (m). Links displacement and time.
Third equation · Acceleration and the Equations of Motionv2=v02​+2aΔxLinks velocity and displacement with no time.
Average of the two velocities · Acceleration and the Equations of MotionΔx=2v+v0​​tValid when the acceleration is constant.
Dropped from rest · Free Fallv=gt,Δy=21​gt2v: speed (m/s), t: time (s), Δy: distance fallen (m), g: free-fall acceleration (m/s2).
Impact speed · Free Fallv2=2gΔyFor an object dropped from rest through a distance.
Maximum height of an upward throw · Free Fallh=2gv02​​v0​: launch speed (m/s), because the velocity at the top is zero.
Time to rise · Free Fallt=gv0​​The total time to return to the launch point is twice this.
Thrown downward · Free Fallv=v0​+gtDown is positive; v0​ is the launch speed downward (m/s).
Reaction distance · Stopping Distance and Timed1​=vt1​v: speed (m/s), t1​: reaction time (s).
Braking distance · Stopping Distance and Timed2​=2av2​a: size of the deceleration (m/s2), without sign.
Braking time · Stopping Distance and Timet2​=av​In seconds.
Total stopping distance · Stopping Distance and Timed=d1​+d2​and the total time is t=t1​+t2​.

Forces and Newton's Laws

Newton's first law · Inertia, the First Law and Net Forceif Fnet​=0 then a=0Velocity stays constant in size and direction: a resting object stays at rest and a moving object keeps its velocity.
Net force on one line · Inertia, the First Law and Net ForceFnet​=Fright​−Fleft​Forces in newtons; a positive result means the net force points right, a negative one means left.
Two perpendicular forces · Inertia, the First Law and Net ForceFnet​=F12​+F22​​Forces in newtons with a right angle between them; for example 32+42​=5N.
Newton's second law · Newton's Second Law, Weight and MassFnet​=maForce in newtons, mass m in kg, acceleration a in m/s2.
Acceleration · Newton's Second Law, Weight and Massa=mFnet​​The direction is that of the net force.
Weight · Newton's Second Law, Weight and MassW=mgWeight W in newtons, mass m in kg, g in m/s2.
Normal force (pressing down on a horizontal surface) · Normal Force and FrictionN=W+Fpress​All in newtons; with no extra press, N=W.
Normal force on a slope · Normal Force and FrictionN=Wcosθθ is the angle of the slope to the horizontal; N and W in newtons.
Maximum static friction · Normal Force and Frictionfs,max​=μs​Nμs​ has no unit. The actual static friction equals the applied force and never exceeds this limit.
Kinetic friction · Normal Force and Frictionfk​=μk​NPoints against the sliding; its value is constant.
Newton's third law · Newton's Third Law: Action and ReactionFA on B​=−FB on A​Equal size, opposite direction, and they never act on the same object.
Tension in a rope lifting an object · Tension, Pulleys and the ElevatorT−W=maUp is positive; T and W in newtons, m in kg, a in m/s2.
Acceleration of two masses over a pulley · Tension, Pulleys and the Elevatora=m1​+m2​(m1​−m2​)g​m1​ is the heavier mass; masses in kg, g and a in m/s2.
Mass on a smooth table joined to a hanging mass · Tension, Pulleys and the Elevatora=m1​+m2​m2​g​m1​ is the mass on the table and m2​ the hanging mass, in kg; a in m/s2.
Scale reading in an elevator · Tension, Pulleys and the ElevatorR=m(g+a)a is positive upward and negative downward; R in newtons.
Acceleration of a falling object in air · Drag and Terminal Velocitya=mW−D​W is weight and D is drag in newtons, m in kg; a in m/s2.
Condition for terminal velocity · Drag and Terminal VelocityD=WThen the net force is zero and the acceleration is zero.

Motion in Two Dimensions and Gravitation

Horizontal component · Vectors: Adding, Resolving and EquilibriumFx​=Fcosθθ is the angle from the horizontal. The component has the same unit as the vector (for example N).
Vertical component · Vectors: Adding, Resolving and EquilibriumFy​=Fsinθθ is the angle from the horizontal. If the angle is measured from the vertical, sine and cosine swap.
Resultant of two perpendicular vectors · Vectors: Adding, Resolving and EquilibriumR=A2+B2​A and B are the two sizes in one unit; R has the same unit.
Direction of the resultant · Vectors: Adding, Resolving and Equilibriumtanθ=AB​θ is the angle between the resultant and vector A when the two vectors are perpendicular. The ratio has no unit.
Equilibrium condition · Vectors: Adding, Resolving and EquilibriumΣF=0Holds separately in the horizontal and in the vertical direction (N).
Height of a horizontal projectile · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and Rangeh=21​gt2h in m, g=10m/s2, t in s. Used to find the fall time.
Horizontal range · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and RangeR=vx​tR in m, vx​ in m/s, t in s.
Horizontal velocity component · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and Rangevx​=vcosθθ is the launch angle above the horizontal. It stays constant (m/s).
Vertical velocity component · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and Rangevy​=vsinθIn m/s; it is zero at the top. Time to rise =vy​÷g.
Maximum height · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and Rangehmax​=2gvy2​​In m, with g=10m/s2.
Range at an angle · Projectiles: Horizontal, Angled and RangeR=gv2sin2θ​For launch from level ground. The greatest range is at θ=45∘.
Component along the surface · The Incline: Weight Components and FrictionW∥​=Wsinθθ is the incline angle. W=mg in N.
Component perpendicular to the surface · The Incline: Weight Components and FrictionW⊥​=WcosθEquals the normal force if no other perpendicular forces act (N).
Acceleration on a smooth incline · The Incline: Weight Components and Frictiona=gsinθg=10m/s2. Independent of mass.
Friction force · The Incline: Weight Components and Frictionf=μNIn N. μ has no unit, and friction opposes the sliding direction.
Acceleration on a rough incline · The Incline: Weight Components and Frictiona=g(sinθ−μcosθ)In m/s2, for an object sliding down.
Period · Circular Motion and Centripetal ForceT=nt​t is the total time in s and n the number of turns; T in s.
Frequency · Circular Motion and Centripetal Forcef=T1​In Hz (turns per second).
Speed on a circle · Circular Motion and Centripetal Forcev=T2πr​r in m and T in s, so v is in m/s.
Centripetal acceleration · Circular Motion and Centripetal Forceac​=rv2​In m/s2, directed toward the centre.
Centripetal force · Circular Motion and Centripetal ForceFc​=mrv2​In N, with m in kg.
Law of universal gravitation · Gravitation and Kepler's LawsF=Gr2m1​m2​​F in N, masses in kg, r is the distance between centres in m, and G=6.67×10−11Nm2/kg2.
Gravitational acceleration · Gravitation and Kepler's Lawsg=Gr2M​In m/s2, with r measured from the planet's centre. It falls with the square of the distance.
Kepler's third law · Gravitation and Kepler's Lawsr3T2​=constantThe same constant for all planets orbiting the same Sun.

Momentum, Energy and Their Conservation

Linear momentum · Linear Momentum and Impulsep=mvm is mass in kg, v is velocity in m/s, and p is momentum in kg·m/s.
Impulse · Linear Momentum and ImpulseJ=FtF is force in N, t is time in s, and J is impulse in N·s (the same as kg·m/s).
Impulse–momentum theorem · Linear Momentum and ImpulseFt=Δp=mvf​−mvi​vf​ and vi​ are final and initial velocities; keep the signs for direction.
Average force · Linear Momentum and ImpulseF=tΔp​F in N, t in s, Δp in kg·m/s. Use this form to find the force in a collision.
Conservation of momentum · Conservation of Momentum and Collisionspbefore​=pafter​The sum of the momenta of all objects before the collision equals the sum after it (with signs for direction).
Perfectly inelastic collision · Conservation of Momentum and Collisionsm1​v1​+m2​v2​=(m1​+m2​)vm is mass in kg, v is velocity in m/s, subscripts 1 and 2 label the objects, and the last v is their common velocity after sticking.
Work · Work and PowerW=FdcosθW in J, F in N, d in m, and θ is the angle between force and displacement.
Power · Work and PowerP=tW​P in W, W in J, t in s. One kilowatt is 1000W.
Power and speed · Work and PowerP=FvFor constant speed: F in N and v in m/s.
Kinetic energy · Kinetic and Potential EnergyKE=21​mv2m in kg, v in m/s, KE in J.
Gravitational potential energy · Kinetic and Potential EnergyPE=mghg≈10m/s2, h is the vertical height in m, PE in J.
Work–energy theorem · Kinetic and Potential EnergyWnet​=ΔKE=KEf​−KEi​Net work and kinetic energy are both in joules.
Conservation of mechanical energy · Conservation of Energy and FrictionKE1​+PE1​=KE2​+PE2​Valid when there is no friction or air resistance; energies in joules, subscripts 1 and 2 for the two points.
Speed after a free fall · Conservation of Energy and Frictionv=2gh​g=10m/s2, h in m, v in m/s.
Energy lost to friction · Conservation of Energy and FrictionElost​=fdf is the friction force in N, d is the distance slid in m, and the result is in J.
Mechanical advantage · Simple Machines and EfficiencyMA=Feffort​Fload​​Both forces in N; the result is a pure number. For an ideal machine it also equals effort distance ÷ load distance.
Efficiency · Simple Machines and Efficiencyefficiency=Win​Wout​​×100Both works in J; efficiency is a percentage, always below 100 for real machines.

Thermal Energy and States of Matter

Converting between scales · Temperature and the Kelvin ScaleT=t+273t is the Celsius temperature in ∘C and T the kelvin temperature in K. To go back, subtract 273.
Temperature change · Temperature and the Kelvin ScaleΔT=ΔtA difference between two temperatures does not change with the conversion, so never add 273 to a difference.
Heat quantity · Heat Quantity and Specific HeatQ=mcΔTQ is heat in J, m mass in kg, c specific heat in J/(kg⋅K), and ΔT the temperature change in K (or ∘C).
Thermal equilibrium · Heat Quantity and Specific HeatQlost​=Qgained​Valid in an insulated container that exchanges no heat with the surroundings; both sides in J.
Heat to melt · Changes of State and Latent HeatQ=mLf​Q in J, m in kg, Lf​ the latent heat of fusion in J/kg. For ice: 3.3×105J/kg.
Heat to vaporize · Changes of State and Latent HeatQ=mLv​Lv​ is the latent heat of vaporization; for boiling water 2.3×106J/kg. The temperature stays constant during vaporization.
Rate of conduction · Modes of Heat TransferP=dkAΔT​P is the rate of heat flow in watts (J/s), k the conductivity in W/(m⋅K), A the area in m2, ΔT the temperature difference across the faces in K, and d the thickness in m.
Linear expansion · Thermal ExpansionΔL=αL0​ΔTα is the coefficient of linear expansion in 1/∘C (or 1/K), L0​ the original length in m, and ΔT the temperature change in K; ΔL comes out in m.
Boyle's law (T constant) · The Gas LawsP1​V1​=P2​V2​Pressure in any unit (for example kPa) and volume in any unit (for example L), as long as both states use the same units.
Charles's law (P constant) · The Gas LawsT1​V1​​=T2​V2​​Temperatures in kelvin, never Celsius. Volume in the same unit on both sides.
Pressure law (V constant) · The Gas LawsT1​P1​​=T2​P2​​Temperatures in kelvin; pressure in the same unit on both sides.
Combined gas law · The Gas LawsT1​P1​V1​​=T2​P2​V2​​Fixed amount of gas, temperatures in kelvin. At constant volume TP​ stays constant.
First law · The First Law of Thermodynamics and EnginesΔU=Q−WAll in joules. Q is positive when the gas absorbs heat, and W is positive when the gas does work.
Isothermal process · The First Law of Thermodynamics and EnginesQ=WThe temperature is constant, so ΔU=0.
Adiabatic process · The First Law of Thermodynamics and EnginesΔU=−WNo heat exchange, so Q=0.
Engine efficiency · The First Law of Thermodynamics and Enginese=Qh​W​×100%W=Qh​−Qc​, with Qh​ the heat absorbed and Qc​ the heat rejected, in joules.

Vibrations, Waves and Sound

Crossing a boundary · Wave Types and How Waves Travelf=λv​Frequency f (Hz) stays constant; speed v (m/s) is set by the medium; if v increases, the wavelength λ (m) increases by the same ratio.
Frequency and period · Wave Properties: Frequency, Period and Wavelengthf=T1​f is the frequency in Hz; T is the period in s.
Wave speed · Wave Properties: Frequency, Period and Wavelengthv=fλv is the speed in m/s; f the frequency in Hz; λ the wavelength in m.
Wavelength · Wave Properties: Frequency, Period and Wavelengthλ=fv​λ is the wavelength in m.
Hooke's law · Hooke's Law, Springs and PendulumsF=kxF is the force in N; k the spring constant in N/m; x the extension in m.
Pendulum period · Hooke's Law, Springs and PendulumsT=2πgL​​T in s; L the length in m; g the gravitational acceleration in m/s² (about 10).
Mass-spring period · Hooke's Law, Springs and PendulumsT=2πkm​​m is the mass in kg; k the spring constant in N/m.
Pendulum length · Hooke's Law, Springs and PendulumsL=4π2gT2​Obtained by squaring the pendulum law and isolating L.
Distance, speed, time · Sound: Echoes, Thunder, Pitch, Loudness and Decibelsd=vtd in m; v in m/s; t in s. Used directly for thunder and lightning.
Obstacle distance in an echo · Sound: Echoes, Thunder, Pitch, Loudness and Decibelsd=2vt​t is the time between the shout and hearing the echo.
Change in sound level · Sound: Echoes, Thunder, Pitch, Loudness and DecibelsΔβ=10logI1​I2​​The change is in dB; I₁ and I₂ are the old and new intensities. Use log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1000 = 3, log 2 ≈ 0.3.
Sound level · Sound: Echoes, Thunder, Pitch, Loudness and Decibelsβ=10logI0​I​β is the level in dB; I is the intensity; I₀ = 10−12W/m2 is the hearing threshold.
Superposition · Superposition and Beatsy=y1​+y2​Displacements are added with their sign: a crest is positive, a trough negative.
Beat frequency · Superposition and Beatsfbeat​=fhigh​−flow​In Hz, which is the number of beats per second.
Harmonics of a string fixed at both ends · Standing Waves and Resonance in Strings and Pipesfn​=nf1​n = 1, 2, 3 ...; frequencies in Hz.
Pipe open at both ends · Standing Waves and Resonance in Strings and Pipesf1​=2Lv​v in m/s and L in m. Harmonics n = 1, 2, 3 ... times f₁.
Pipe closed at one end · Standing Waves and Resonance in Strings and Pipesf1​=4Lv​Only odd harmonics exist: n = 1, 3, 5 ... times f₁.

Light: Reflection and Refraction

Law of reflection · Reflection and the Plane Mirrorangle of reflection=angle of incidenceBoth angles are in degrees and measured from the normal to the surface.
Image distance · Reflection and the Plane Mirrordi​=do​Both are measured from the mirror surface in metres; the object is in front, the image behind.
Focal length · Spherical Mirrors: Concave and Convexf=2R​f is the focal length and R the radius of curvature, both in cm or m.
Mirror equation · Spherical Mirrors: Concave and Convexf1​=do​1​+di​1​do​ is the object distance, di​ the image distance, f the focal length, all in the same length unit.
Magnification · Spherical Mirrors: Concave and Convexm=−do​di​​=ho​hi​​No unit; hi​ and ho​ are image and object heights. A negative sign means inverted.
Refractive index · Refraction, Refractive Index and Snell’s Lawn=speed of light in the mediumspeed of light in vacuum​n has no unit; the speed of light in vacuum is 3×108m/s.
Snell’s law · Refraction, Refractive Index and Snell’s Lawn1​sinθ1​=n2​sinθ2​n1​ and n2​ are the indices of the two media; θ1​ and θ2​ are the angles of incidence and refraction, measured from the normal.
Wavelength in a medium · Refraction, Refractive Index and Snell’s Lawλmedium​=nλair​​In nm or m; the frequency does not change.
Critical angle between two media · Total Internal Reflection and Optical Fibressinθc​=n1​n2​​n1​ is the index of the denser medium (where the light travels), the larger one; n2​ is the index of the other; θc​ is the critical angle.
Critical angle with air · Total Internal Reflection and Optical Fibressinθc​=n1​n is the refractive index of the material; air has index 1.
Lens equation · Lenses: Convex and Concavef1​=do​1​+di​1​f is the focal length, do​ the object distance and di​ the image distance, in one length unit (cm or m).
Magnification · Lenses: Convex and Concavem=−do​di​​=ho​hi​​No unit; negative means inverted, positive means upright.
Lens power · Lenses: Convex and ConcaveP=f1​P is in dioptres and f in metres. For example f=0.5m gives 2 dioptres.
Two lenses in contact · Lenses: Convex and ConcaveP=P1​+P2​In dioptres, keeping the sign of each lens.
Constructive interference · The Wave Nature and Properties of Lightpath difference=m×λm=0,1,2,… and λ is the wavelength, in the same length unit.
Destructive interference · The Wave Nature and Properties of Lightpath difference=(m+0.5)×λm=0,1,2,… and λ is the wavelength.
Fringe spacing · The Wave Nature and Properties of LightΔy=dλL​λ is the wavelength, L the distance from slits to screen, d the slit separation; all in metres.
Illuminance · The Wave Nature and Properties of LightE=r2I​E is illuminance in lux, I the source intensity, r the distance from the source in metres.
Power of the correcting lens · The Eye, Nearsightedness and the Compound MicroscopeP=f1​P is in dioptres and f in metres; a concave lens has negative f, so negative power.
Total magnification of the microscope · The Eye, Nearsightedness and the Compound Microscopemtotal​=mobjective​×meyepiece​Each magnification has no unit.

Static and Current Electricity

Charge quantisation · Electric Charge and Ways of ChargingQ=n×1.6×10−19Cn is the number of extra or missing electrons (a whole number); Q is in coulombs.
Contact between identical spheres · Electric Charge and Ways of ChargingQfinal​=2Q1​+Q2​​Two identical spheres share their total charge equally after touching; keep the signs of Q1​ and Q2​.
Coulomb's law · Coulomb's Law and the Electric FieldF=kr2q1​q2​​F in newtons, q1​,q2​ in coulombs, r the distance in metres, k=9×109Nm2/C2.
Electric field strength · Coulomb's Law and the Electric FieldE=qF​E in N/C, F in newtons, q the test charge in coulombs.
Field of a point charge · Coulomb's Law and the Electric FieldE=kr2Q​Q is the source charge in coulombs, r the distance from it in metres.
Force on a charge in a field · Coulomb's Law and the Electric FieldF=qEF in newtons, q in coulombs, E in N/C.
Potential difference · Potential Difference, Work and the Uniform FieldV=qW​V in volts, W the work in joules, q the charge in coulombs.
Work and voltage · Potential Difference, Work and the Uniform FieldW=qVW in joules, q in coulombs, V in volts.
Uniform field between plates · Potential Difference, Work and the Uniform FieldE=dV​E in V/m (equal to N/C), V the voltage across the plates, d the separation in metres.
Kinetic energy gained · Potential Difference, Work and the Uniform FieldEk​=qVFor a charge released from rest. Ek​ in joules, q in coulombs, V in volts.
Capacitance · Capacitors and CapacitanceC=VQ​C in farads, Q in coulombs, V in volts.
Stored energy · Capacitors and CapacitanceU=21​CV2U in joules, C in farads, V in volts.
Capacitors in parallel · Capacitors and CapacitanceCtotal​=C1​+C2​The voltage is the same across each capacitor; the charges add.
Two capacitors in series · Capacitors and CapacitanceCtotal​=C1​+C2​C1​C2​​The charge is the same on each capacitor; the voltage is shared. The total is smaller than the smallest capacitor. In general Ctotal​1​=C1​1​+C2​1​.
Current · Current, Ohm's Law and ResistanceI=tQ​I in amperes, Q in coulombs, t in seconds.
Ohm's law · Current, Ohm's Law and ResistanceV=IRV in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms.
Resistance of a wire · Current, Ohm's Law and ResistanceR=ρAL​R in ohms, ρ the resistivity of the material (in Ωm), L the length in metres, A the cross-section area in m2.
Current with internal resistance · Current, Ohm's Law and ResistanceI=R+rε​ε is the emf in volts, R the external resistance and r the internal resistance, both in ohms.
Terminal voltage · Current, Ohm's Law and ResistanceV=ε−IrV is the voltage across the battery terminals in volts, I the current in amperes.
Equivalent resistance in series · Combining Resistors and Kirchhoff's RulesRtotal​=R1​+R2​+R3​Resistances in ohms. The current is the same through all; the voltages add up to the total.
Two resistors in parallel · Combining Resistors and Kirchhoff's RulesRtotal​=R1​+R2​R1​R2​​Resistances in ohms. The voltage is the same across both, and the currents add. n equal resistors of value R in parallel give nR​. In general Rtotal​1​=R1​1​+R2​1​.
Junction rule · Combining Resistors and Kirchhoff's Rules∑Iin​=∑Iout​Currents in amperes at any branching point.
Loop rule · Combining Resistors and Kirchhoff's Rules∑ε=∑IRAround a closed loop, in volts.
Electric power · Electric Power, Energy and Household CircuitsP=IVP in watts, I in amperes, V in volts.
Two other forms of power · Electric Power, Energy and Household CircuitsP=I2R=RV2​R in ohms. Use the first when the current is fixed and the second when the voltage is fixed.
Electrical energy · Electric Power, Energy and Household CircuitsE=PtE in joules when P is in watts and t in seconds, or in kilowatt-hours when P is in kilowatts and t in hours.
Heat produced by current · Electric Power, Energy and Household CircuitsQ=I2RtQ in joules, I in amperes, R in ohms, t in seconds.

Magnetism and Electromagnetism

Pole rule · Magnets and Field Linesunlike poles→attractUnlike poles attract; like poles repel.
Field of a long straight wire in air · The Magnetic Field of a CurrentB=r2×10−7I​B field in T, I current in A, r distance from the wire in m.
Field of a solenoid · The Magnetic Field of a CurrentB=4π×10−7nIB field in T, n = turns per metre (number of turns divided by length in m), I current in A.
Force on a wire · Magnetic Force on a Wire and on a ChargeF=BILsinθF in N, B in T, I in A, L length in m, θ angle between wire and field. At 90∘, sinθ=1.
Force on a charge · Magnetic Force on a Wire and on a ChargeF=qvBsinθF in N, q in C, v in m/s, B in T, θ angle between velocity and field.
Radius of the path · Magnetic Force on a Wire and on a Charger=qBmv​r in m, m in kg, v in m/s, q in C, B in T (velocity perpendicular to the field).
Faraday's law · Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's LawE=NΔtΔΦ​E emf in V, N number of turns, ΔΦ change of flux in Wb, Δt time in s. (The minus sign in the full law expresses Lenz’s law.)
Flux · Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's LawΦ=BAcosθΦ in Wb, B in T, A area in m2, θ angle between the field and the normal to the surface.
Motional emf · Electromagnetic Induction and Faraday's LawE=BLvE in V, B in T, L rod length in m, v in m/s (motion perpendicular to the field).
Voltage ratio · Generators, Motors and TransformersVp​Vs​​=Np​Ns​​Vs​,Vp​ secondary and primary voltages in V; Ns​,Np​ numbers of turns (ideal transformer).
Power conservation · Generators, Motors and TransformersVp​Ip​=Vs​Is​Voltage in V, current in A, power in W. So currents are inversely proportional to voltages.
Wave speed · The Electromagnetic Spectrumc=fλc=3×108m/s, f frequency in Hz, λ wavelength in m.

Modern Physics: Quantum, Atom and Nucleus

Photon energy · Photon Energy and the Photoelectric EffectE=hfh=6.6×10−34J⋅s (Planck's constant), f in Hz, E in J.
Photon energy from wavelength · Photon Energy and the Photoelectric EffectE=λhc​c=3×108m/s, λ in m.
Einstein's equation · Photon Energy and the Photoelectric EffectKEmax​=hf−ϕϕ is the work function. All three terms must use the same unit (all J or all eV).
Threshold frequency · Photon Energy and the Photoelectric Effectϕ=hf0​At f0​ the photon energy equals the work function exactly, so the kinetic energy is zero.
Stopping potential · Photon Energy and the Photoelectric EffectVs​(V)=KEmax​(eV)The numbers are equal; the units differ.
Momentum · Matter Waves (de Broglie)p=mvm in kg, v in m/s, p in kg⋅m/s.
de Broglie wavelength · Matter Waves (de Broglie)λ=ph​h=6.6×10−34J⋅s, λ in m.
Level energy in hydrogen · Energy Levels and Bohr TransitionsEn​=n2−13.6​eVn is the level number (1, 2, 3, ...).
Photon energy in a transition · Energy Levels and Bohr TransitionsEphoton​=Ehigh​−Elow​Take the gap between the two levels; it is always positive, for absorption and emission alike.
Photon wavelength · Energy Levels and Bohr Transitionsλ=Ephoton​hc​Energy in joules, wavelength in metres; a smaller energy means a longer wavelength.
Number of neutrons · Nuclear Structure and Radioactive DecayN=A−ZA is the mass number (nucleons), Z is the atomic number (protons).
Alpha decay · Nuclear Structure and Radioactive DecayXZA​X2Z2A​X​XZ−2A−4​X2Z−2​2A−4​Y+X24​X2224​HeMass number falls by 4, atomic number by 2.

Chemistry

Atoms and the Periodic Table

Number of neutrons · Atomic Structure, Isotopes and Ionsneutrons=mass number−atomic numberMass number = protons + neutrons; atomic number = number of protons.
Average atomic mass · Atomic Structure, Isotopes and Ionsatomic mass=(m1​×a1​)+(m2​×a2​)m is the isotope mass in u and a its abundance as a decimal, so 20% is 0.2. The abundances add to 1.
Electrons in an ion · Atomic Structure, Isotopes and Ionselectrons=atomic number−chargeThe charge is positive for a positive ion and negative for a negative ion, so MgX2+ has charge +2.
Wavelength and frequency · Light, Atomic Spectra and the Bohr Modelc=λfc=3×108m/s is the speed of light, λ the wavelength in m, f the frequency in Hz.
Photon energy · Light, Atomic Spectra and the Bohr ModelE=hfh=6.6×10−34J⋅s is Planck's constant, f the frequency in Hz, E the energy in J. Energy is proportional to frequency.
Orbitals in a sublevel · Quantum Numbers and Electron Configurationorbitals=2ℓ+1ℓ is the secondary quantum number: s (ℓ=0) gives 1, p (ℓ=1) gives 3, d (ℓ=2) gives 5.
Maximum electrons in a principal level · Quantum Numbers and Electron Configurationmaximum=2n2n is the principal quantum number: level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 8, level 3 holds 18, level 4 holds 32.
Period number · Organising the Periodic Table and Locating Elementsperiod=highest principal levelExample: a configuration ending in 3p5 is in period 3.
Group number in the p block · Organising the Periodic Table and Locating Elementsgroup=10+valence electronsValence electrons are the s and p electrons of the last level. In the s block the group number equals the valence electrons directly.
Successive ionization energies · Periodic Trends: Radius, Ionization Energy and Electronegativityvalence electrons=number of energies before the big jumpIonization energy is measured in kJ/mol. Look for the first big jump between two successive energies.
Mass left after half-lives · Radioactivity and Nuclear Decaym=m0​(21​)km0​ is the starting mass, m the mass left (same unit), and k the number of half-lives.
Number of half-lives · Radioactivity and Nuclear Decayk=t1/2​t​t is the total time and t1/2​ the half-life, in the same unit (seconds, days or years).

Chemical Bonding and Molecules

Electronegativity difference · Bond types and bond polarityΔEN=ENlarger​−ENsmaller​Subtract the smaller electronegativity from the larger one (no unit), so the result is never negative.
Neutral ionic compound · Ions and ionic compoundscount+​×charge+​=count−​×∣charge−​∣Compare the size of the charges: adjust the number of each ion until both sides are equal, so the compound is neutral.
Number of pairs in a molecule · Lewis structures and multiple bondspairs=2total valence electrons​Bonding pairs plus lone pairs in the final drawing must equal this number.
Number of electron groups · Molecular shapes and bond anglesgroups=bonded atoms+lone pairsA double or triple bond counts as one group. This number sets the general arrangement of the pairs.

Percent by mass · Percent composition by mass%=molar mass of compoundmass of element in one mole​×100Masses in grams; the result is a percentage.

Multiplier · Empirical and molecular formulasx=molar mass of empirical formulamolar mass of molecule​x is a whole number; molecular formula = empirical formula × x.
Mole ratio · Stoichiometry: moles, mass and volumenwanted​=ngiven​×coefficient of givencoefficient of wanted​Coefficients come from the balanced equation.
Moles · Stoichiometry: moles, mass and volumen=Mm​m mass in grams, M molar mass in g/mol.
Gas volume · Stoichiometry: moles, mass and volumeV=n×22.4LLitres, at standard conditions.

Charles's law · Boyle's and Charles's LawsT1​V1​​=T2​V2​​V is volume (L), T is temperature in kelvin. Pressure and amount of gas are constant.
Gay-Lussac's law · Gay-Lussac's Law and the Combined Gas LawT1​P1​​=T2​P2​​P is pressure (atm), T is temperature in kelvin. Volume and amount of gas are constant.
Combined gas law · Gay-Lussac's Law and the Combined Gas LawT1​P1​V1​​=T2​P2​V2​​V is volume (L). The amount of gas is constant and temperature is in kelvin.
Avogadro's law · Avogadro, Molar Volume and the Ideal Gas Lawn1​V1​​=n2​V2​​V is volume (L), n is moles. Temperature and pressure are constant.

Dalton's law · Dalton's Law of Partial PressuresPtotal​=PA​+PB​+PC​P is pressure in atm. Each term is the partial pressure of one gas.
Partial pressure · Dalton's Law of Partial PressuresPA​=ntotal​nA​​×Ptotal​n is moles, and the fraction is the mole fraction of gas A.

Energy and Reaction Rates

Change in enthalpy · Energy in Reactions: Exothermic and EndothermicΔH=Hproducts​−Hreactants​Energy in kJ. A negative result means exothermic; a positive result means endothermic.
Heat from moles · Energy in Reactions: Exothermic and Endothermicq=ΔHper mol​×nq in kJ, ΔH per mole in kJ/mol, n in mol. n=mass÷molar mass (g divided by g/mol).
Specific heat law · Specific Heatq=m×c×ΔTq heat in J, m mass in g, c specific heat in J/(g⋅∘C), ΔT temperature change in ∘C.
Finding the temperature change · Specific HeatΔT=m×cq​Divide the heat by the product of mass and specific heat; the result is in ∘C.
Finding the specific heat · Specific Heatc=m×ΔTq​Heat in J and mass in g; the result is in J/(g⋅∘C).
Hess's law · Hess's Law and Enthalpy of FormationΔHtotal​=ΔH1​+ΔH2​+…All values in kJ. The direct route and the stepwise route give the same value.
ΔH from formation enthalpies · Hess's Law and Enthalpy of FormationΔH=∑nΔHf​(products)−∑nΔHf​(reactants)Multiply each formation enthalpy (kJ/mol) by its moles in the equation. ΔHf​ of a standard-state element is 0.
ΔH from bond energies · Bond EnergiesΔH=∑Ebonds broken​−∑Ebonds formed​All energies in kJ. Negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic.
Average rate · Reaction Rate and the Rate Lawrate=Δt∣Δ[conc]∣​Concentration in mol/L, time in s; rate in mol/(L⋅s).
Rate law · Reaction Rate and the Rate Lawrate=k[A]m[B]nk is the rate constant, a value that belongs to the reaction and the temperature. m and n are found by experiment. Overall order = m+n.
Forward activation energy · Collision Theory, Activation Energy and CatalystsEa​=Epeak​−Ereactants​Energy in kJ. For the reverse reaction subtract the products energy instead.
Change in enthalpy · Collision Theory, Activation Energy and CatalystsΔH=Eproducts​−Ereactants​Not affected by a catalyst.
Rule of thumb for temperature · Factors Affecting Rate: Surface Area, Temperature and Concentrationnew rate=old rate×2ΔT/10ΔT is the rise in ∘C. A rough rule: every 10∘C doubles the rate. The time to finish is inversely proportional to the rate.

Chemical Equilibrium

Condition for equilibrium · Dynamic Equilibrium and Catalystsforward rate=reverse rateEach rate is measured in mol/L per second. When they are equal, concentrations stay constant.
Equilibrium constant · The Equilibrium Expression, Pure Substances and Solubility ProductK=[reactants]coefficients[products]coefficients​Square brackets mean concentration in mol/L; exponents are the coefficients of the balanced equation. Pure solids and liquids are not written.

Reversing the equation · Calculating and Manipulating KKnew​=K1​The new constant belongs to the reversed equation at the same temperature.
Multiplying coefficients by n · Calculating and Manipulating KKnew​=Knn may be a fraction, such as one half when coefficients are divided by two.
Adding two equations · Calculating and Manipulating KKtotal​=K1​×K2​Add the equations and cancel substances that appear on both sides.
Reaction quotient · Meaning of K and the Reaction QuotientQ=[reactants]coefficients[products]coefficients​Calculated from the present concentrations in mol/L, not from equilibrium concentrations.

Biology

Cell Structure and Function

Levels of organisation · Cell Theory and Types of Cellscell→tissue→organ→organ system→organismEach level is made of groups of the level before it; the cell is the base.
Order of the secretion pathway · Golgi Apparatus, Lysosomes, Vacuoles and the Secretion Pathwayribosome→rough ER→Golgi→membraneVesicles carry the material between stations; at the end it leaves by exocytosis.
Photosynthesis · Mitochondria and Chloroplasts6COX2​+6HX2​O​CX6​HX12​OX6​+6OX2​Needs light and chlorophyll in the chloroplast.
Cellular respiration · Mitochondria and ChloroplastsCX6​HX12​OX6​+6OX2​​6COX2​+6HX2​OEnergy is released and stored in ATP; most of it happens in the mitochondria.
Direction of water · Passive Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis and Tonicitywater: from lower solute→to higher soluteThe solute stays put and water crosses the membrane until the two sides balance.
One pump cycle · Active Transport and Vesicle TransportATP→3 Na out+2 K inEach ATP pushes three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.

Cellular Energy

Using ATP · ATP and Cell EnergyATP→ADP+P+energyOne phosphate group (P) leaves and the energy is used for cell work.
Renewing ATP · ATP and Cell EnergyADP+P+energy→ATPThe energy comes from cellular respiration, or from light in photosynthesis.
How an enzyme works · Enzymesenzyme+substrate→complex→enzyme+productThe enzyme comes out as it was, ready for a new substrate.
Photosynthesis equation · Photosynthesis and the Light Reactions6COX2​+6HX2​O​CX6​HX12​OX6​+6OX2​It occurs in the presence of light. Six CO2 give one glucose and six oxygen molecules.

Needed to build one glucose · The Calvin Cycle6COX2​+18ATP+12NADPH→glucoseThe cycle turns six times to build one glucose; each turn needs one COX2​, 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
Aerobic respiration equation · Aerobic Cellular RespirationCX6​HX12​OX6​+6OX2​​6COX2​+6HX2​OWith energy, part of which is stored in ATP. All the carbon leaves as COX2​.
Glycolysis · Aerobic Cellular Respirationglucose→2 pyruvate+2 ATP (net)+2 NADHIn the cytoplasm, without oxygen.

Mendelian and Complex Inheritance

Results of Aa×Aa · Punnett Squares, Ratios and Probability1:2:1 genotype and 3:1 phenotypeComplete dominance; the recessive appearance is in a quarter of the offspring.

Probability · Punnett Squares, Ratios and ProbabilityProbability=all boxeswanted boxes​Boxes from a Punnett square.

Number of gamete types · Dihybrid Crosses and Independent Assortment2nn: number of hybrid gene pairs; AaBb has two, so 22=4 gametes.

Carrier mother and affected father · Sex Determination and Sex-Linked TraitsXBXb×XbYThe four boxes are equally likely: a carrier daughter, an affected daughter, a normal son and an affected son, 41​ each.

Molecular Genetics and Biotechnology

Chargaff's rule (1) · Structure of DNA and RNAA=TThe percentage (or number) of adenine equals that of thymine in double-stranded DNA.
Chargaff's rule (2) · Structure of DNA and RNAG=CThe percentage (or number) of guanine equals that of cytosine.
Sum of percentages · Structure of DNA and RNAA+T+G+C=100%The four base percentages of double-stranded DNA add up to the whole.
Number of molecules after replication · DNA Replicationmolecules=2nn: the number of times one molecule replicates.
Old strands · DNA Replicationmolecules holding an old strand=2One original molecule has only two old strands, so they sit in only two molecules however many rounds follow.
Length of mature mRNA · Transcription and mRNA Processingmature=sum of exonsLength is counted in nucleotides, and introns are not counted.
Number of possible codons · Translation and the Genetic Codecodons=43=64Four bases at each of the three positions of a codon.
Protein length · Translation and the Genetic Codeamino acids=3nucleotides​−1Nucleotides: the count from the start codon to the end of the stop codon. Subtract 1 because the stop codon adds no amino acid.
Copies after n cycles · Biotechnologycopies=2nn: the number of PCR cycles, starting from one molecule.
Number of fragments · Biotechnologyfragments=cut sites+1For linear DNA. For a circular plasmid the number of fragments equals the number of cut sites.

Classification and Diversity of Life

Virus multiplication in the lytic cycle · Viruses and Their Two Cyclesnew viruses=infected cells×yield per cellYield per cell is the number of new viruses released when one cell bursts.
Proportion of survivors · Natural Selection and Antibiotic Resistanceproportion=totalsurvivors​Survivors and total are both counts of individuals; compare the proportion before and after selection to see which trait increases.

Plant Structure and Function

What the vascular cambium does · Plant tissues, root and leafvascular cambium→secondary xylem (inward)+secondary phloem (outward)The vascular cambium is a meristem between xylem and phloem; it adds wood toward the centre and phloem outward, so the trunk thickens.
Where growth comes from · Plant tissues, root and leafapical meristem→more lengthMeristems at root and shoot tips add length; the vascular cambium adds thickness.
Direction of transport in xylem · Water and food transport, transpiration and stomataXylem: roots→leavesCarries water and minerals upward only, by transpiration pull and water cohesion.
Direction of transport in phloem · Water and food transport, transpiration and stomataPhloem: leaves→other plant partsCarries the sugars made in leaves to where food is used or stored.
What raises transpiration · Water and food transport, transpiration and stomatahigher heat+dryness+wind→more transpirationThese speed up water vapour leaving the leaf; high humidity slows it.
Opening a stoma · Water and food transport, transpiration and stomataguard cells fill with water→swell→stoma openLosing water makes them shrink and the stoma closes.
Phototropism · Plant hormones and tropismsmore auxin on shaded side→longer cells→bend toward lightThe lit side has less auxin, so it lengthens less.
Apical dominance · Plant hormones and tropismscut terminal bud→no auxin→side buds growIt is the terminal bud's auxin that holds back the side buds.
Naming a tropism · Plant hormones and tropismsgrowth toward stimulus=positive tropismGrowth away from the stimulus is a negative tropism. The root is positive to gravity; the stem is negative to it.
Making spores · Plant groups and alternation of generationssporophyte (2n)→spores (n)By meiosis; spores grow into the gametophyte (n).
Making gametes · Plant groups and alternation of generationsgametophyte (n)→gametes (n)By mitosis, so the chromosome set does not change.
Fertilization · Plant groups and alternation of generationsgamete (n)+gamete (n)→zygote (2n)The zygote grows into the sporophyte.
Monocot · Monocots and dicotsone cotyledon→parallel veins+scattered bundlesFlower parts in multiples of 3; fibrous roots.
Dicot · Monocots and dicotstwo cotyledons→net veins+ring of bundlesFlower parts in multiples of 4 or 5; taproot.
Making the zygote · Flower, double fertilization, fruit and germinationsperm nucleus (n)+egg (n)→zygote (2n)The zygote grows into the embryo.
Making the endosperm · Flower, double fertilization, fruit and germinationsperm nucleus (n)+two polar nuclei (n+n)→endosperm (3n)It stores food and feeds the embryo.
After fertilization · Flower, double fertilization, fruit and germinationovule→seed,ovary→fruitThe fruit protects the seeds and helps spread them.

Principles of Ecology

10% rule · Energy Flow: Chains, Webs and PyramidsEnergy passed on=Energy available×101​Energy in kilojoules; "available" is the energy of the lower level, "passed on" is what reaches the next level.
Population density · Populations and Their GrowthDensity=AreaNumber of individuals​Number of individuals as a count, area in square kilometers or square meters; the result is individuals per unit area.
Change in population size · Populations and Their GrowthNew size=Size+(Births+Immigrants)−(Deaths+Emigrants)All terms are counts of individuals over the same time period.
Population growth rate · Populations and Their GrowthGrowth rate=SizeBirths−Deaths​×100Births, deaths and size as counts of individuals over the same period, without migration; the result is a percentage.

Circulation, Respiration, Digestion and Excretion

Cardiac output · The Heart, Vessels and CirculationCardiac output=Heart rate×Stroke volumeCardiac output in mL or L per minute, heart rate in beats per minute, stroke volume in mL per beat. 1000 mL = 1 L.
Minute ventilation · Breathing: Air In and Air OutMinute ventilation=Breaths per minute×Volume per breathBreaths per minute, volume of one breath in mL, result in mL per minute.
Cellular respiration · Breathing: Air In and Air OutCX6​HX12​OX6​+6OX2​​6COX2​+6HX2​OGlucose and oxygen give carbon dioxide and water, and energy is released and stored in ATP.
Carbon dioxide transport reaction · Blood and Gas TransportCOX2​+HX2​O​HX2​COX3​​HX++HCOX3​X−Most carbon dioxide becomes bicarbonate in the plasma, and the released hydrogen ion lowers pH.
Percent reabsorbed · Excretion: the Kidney and FiltrationPercent=FiltrateFiltrate−Urine​×100Filtrate and urine in litres per day; the result is a percentage.

Control, Coordination and Immunity

The reflex arc · Neuron Structure and the Nervous Systemreceptor→sensory neuron→spinal cord→motor neuron→effectorThe spinal cord is the relay centre (an interneuron); the effector is a muscle or a gland.
Stages of the action potential · The Nerve Impulse: Resting Potential, Action Potential and the Synapserest→depolarization→repolarization→restDepolarization is NaX+ entering; repolarization is KX+ leaving.
The pump in each cycle · The Nerve Impulse: Resting Potential, Action Potential and the Synapse3 Na out,2 K inThe pump needs ATP energy because it moves ions against their concentration gradients.
The thyroxine chain · Endocrine Glands and Hormonesiodine→thyroxine→higher metabolic rateLack of iodine lowers thyroxine, raises thyroid-stimulating hormone, and the gland swells.
Insulin control · Blood Glucose, Feedback and Diabetesglucose rises→insulin released→glucose fallsNegative feedback.
Glucagon control · Blood Glucose, Feedback and Diabetesglucose falls→glucagon released→glucose risesAlso negative feedback.
Humoral sequence · Adaptive Immunity: Antigens, T Cells and B Cellsantigen→helper T cell→B cell→antibodiesThe B cell also produces memory cells.

The Nature of Science and the Scientific Method

Writing a hypothesis · The Nature of Science: Hypothesis, Theory and LawIf we change … then …A useful pattern: name the variable you change and the result you will measure.
Rule of a fair test · Designing an Experiment: Variables and the Control Groupreliable test=one independent variable+control group+controlled variables+repeatsChange one thing, compare with a control group, keep the rest constant, and repeat with a large sample.
Mean · Analysing Data and GraphsMean=number of valuessum of values​The values are measurements in the same unit, and the mean has that same unit.
Percent change · Analysing Data and GraphsPercent change=old valuenew value−old value​×100The result is in percent (%); positive means an increase, negative a decrease.
Total magnification · The Microscope and Scientific UnitsTotal=eyepiece×objectiveBoth powers are plain numbers (times of enlargement).
Real size · The Microscope and Scientific UnitsReal size=magnificationimage size​Image size and real size are in the same unit of length.
Useful conversions · The Microscope and Scientific Units1mm=1000μmAlso: 1cm=10mm, 1L=1000mL, 1kg=1000g.

Support, Movement and Human Reproduction

Sarcomeres in a fibre · Muscles: Types and How They Contractfibre shortening=shortening of one sarcomere×number of sarcomeres in a rowSarcomeres are joined end to end, so their small shortenings add up to the shortening of the fibre.
Chromosomes in the zygote · Fertilizationzygote chromosomes=23+23=46The sperm gives 23 chromosomes and the egg gives 23.

Shifted parabola · Parabolas(x−h)2=4p(y−k)Vertex (h,k), focus (h,k+p) and directrix y=k−p.
Ellipse with a horizontal major axis · Ellipses and Circlesa2x2​+b2y2​=1a is half the major axis and b half the minor axis (length units), with a>b.
Distance from a focus to the centre · Ellipses and Circlesc2=a2−b2c is the distance from each focus to the centre; subtract for an ellipse.
Eccentricity · Ellipses and Circleseccentricity=ac​A number without units between 0 and 1; c is the focus-to-centre distance and a is half the major axis.
Equation of a circle · Ellipses and Circles(x−h)2+(y−k)2=r2Centre (h,k) and radius r.
Hyperbola with horizontal branches · Hyperbolasa2x2​−b2y2​=1Vertices (±a,0) and foci (±c,0); a, b, c are lengths.
Distance from a focus to the centre · Hyperbolasc2=a2+b2Add for a hyperbola; it does not matter whether a is larger than b.
Asymptotes · Hyperbolasy=±ab​xFor horizontal branches; for vertical branches use y=±ba​x.
Parabola · Identifying Conic Sectionsy2=4pxOnly one variable is squared.
Ellipse · Identifying Conic Sectionsa2x2​+b2y2​=1Two squares with the same sign and different coefficients.
Circle · Identifying Conic Sectionsx2+y2=r2Two squares with the same sign and equal coefficients.
Hyperbola · Identifying Conic Sectionsa2x2​−b2y2​=1Two squares with opposite signs.
Vector from A to B · Vectors in the Plane(x2​−x1​,y2​−y1​)End minus start, component by component.
Length of a vector · Vectors in the Planex2+y2​x and y are the components; the length has the same units.
Direction angle · Vectors in the Planetanθ=xy​θ is the angle with the positive x-axis; check which quadrant the vector is in.
Unit vector · Vectors in the Plane(x2+y2​x​,x2+y2​y​)The vector divided by its length; its length is 1.
Condition for parallel vectors · Vectors in the Planex1​y2​=y1​x2​The vectors (x1​,y1​) and (x2​,y2​) are parallel.
Dot product by components · The Dot Producta⋅b=x1​x2​+y1​y2​(x1​,y1​) are the components of a and (x2​,y2​) those of b; the result is a number.
Dot product by the angle · The Dot Producta⋅b=∣a∣∣b∣cosθ∣a∣ and ∣b∣ are the lengths of the vectors and θ is the angle between them.
Angle between two vectors · The Dot Productcosθ=∣a∣∣b∣a⋅b​Divide the dot product by the product of the lengths.
Condition for perpendicular vectors · The Dot Producta⋅b=0For non-zero vectors, the angle between them is 90∘.
Length of the projection · The Dot Product∣b∣a⋅b​The length of the projection of a along b, in the same length units; it is negative when the angle is obtuse.
Length of a vector in space · Vectors in Spacex2+y2+z2​x, y and z are the components of the vector.
Dot product in space · Vectors in Spacex1​x2​+y1​y2​+z1​z2​The result is a number, and it is zero for perpendicular vectors.
Cross product · Vectors in Spacea×b=(y1​z2​−z1​y2​,z1​x2​−x1​z2​,x1​y2​−y1​x2​)The result is a vector perpendicular to both a and b.
Length of the cross product · Vectors in Space∣a×b∣=∣a∣∣b∣sinθθ is the angle between the vectors; the result is the area of the parallelogram with sides a and b, in area units.

Probability and Statistics

Simple probability · Simple probability, sample spaces and geometric probabilityP(A)=number of all outcomesnumber of favourable outcomes​P(A): probability of event A, a number from 0 to 1.
Complement · Simple probability, sample spaces and geometric probabilityP(not A)=1−P(A)The probability that A does not happen.
Geometric probability · Simple probability, sample spaces and geometric probabilityP(A)=total areafavourable area​Use the same square unit on top and bottom (or lengths in one unit).
Factorial · Permutations, combinations and probabilityn!=n×(n−1)×(n−2)×…×2×1Read "n factorial". By convention 0!=1.
Permutations · Permutations, combinations and probabilitypermutations=(n−r)!n!​=n×(n−1)×…n is the number of items and r how many are chosen; write r factors in the product.
Combinations · Permutations, combinations and probabilitycombinations=r!×(n−r)!n!​=r!permutations​Divide by the number of orderings of r items, which is r!.
Independent events · Events: independent, exclusive and conditional probabilityP(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B)Probability that both happen.
Dependent events · Events: independent, exclusive and conditional probabilityP(A∩B)=P(A)×P(B∣A)P(B | A): probability of B after A has happened.
Mutually exclusive · Events: independent, exclusive and conditional probabilityP(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)Probability that one of them happens.
Overlapping events · Events: independent, exclusive and conditional probabilityP(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B)Subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice.
Conditional probability · Events: independent, exclusive and conditional probabilityP(B∣A)=P(A)P(A∩B)​The denominator is the known event A.
Mean · Measures of centre: mean, median and modemean=number of valuessum of values​Add all values, then divide by how many there are.
Mean from a frequency table · Measures of centre: mean, median and modemean=sum of frequenciessum of (value×frequency)​Frequency: how many times the value appears.
Combined mean · Measures of centre: mean, median and modemean=total numbersum of both totals​Each group total = its mean × its size.
Range · Measures of spread: range, variance and standard deviationrange=largest−smallestIn the unit of the data.
Variance · Measures of spread: range, variance and standard deviationvariance=number of valuessum of squared deviations​Deviation: value minus mean. The unit of variance is the square of the data unit.
Standard deviation · Measures of spread: range, variance and standard deviationstandard deviation=variance​Same unit as the data.
Percentage · Reading data from tables and graphspercentage=grand totalfrequency​×100Frequency of the category divided by the sum of frequencies.
Percentage change · Reading data from tables and graphspercentage change=first valuedifference​×100Difference = new value minus first value.
Expected value · Distributions: probability, binomial and normalexpected value=sum of (value×probability)All probabilities add to 1.
Binomial · Distributions: probability, binomial and normalP=ways×pk×(1−p)n−kn: trials, k: successes, p: success probability per trial; ways counted by combinations.
Expected successes (binomial) · Distributions: probability, binomial and normalmean=n×pn: number of trials; p: success probability in one trial.
Z-score · Distributions: probability, binomial and normalz=standard deviationvalue−mean​Positive above the mean, negative below.

Limits and Derivatives

Definition of a limit · The idea of a limit and estimating itlimx→a​f(x)=LL is the number f(x) approaches as x approaches a.
Condition for a limit to exist · The idea of a limit and estimating itlimx→a−​f(x)=limx→a+​f(x)The left and right limits must be equal; if they differ, the limit does not exist.
Limit laws · Evaluating limits algebraicallylim(f+g)=limf+limgThe limit of a sum, difference or product equals the sum, difference or product of the limits.
Limit of a quotient · Evaluating limits algebraicallylimgf​=limglimf​Provided limg=0.
Difference of squares · Evaluating limits algebraicallyx2−b2=(x−b)(x+b)x and b are numbers.
Difference of cubes · Evaluating limits algebraicallyx3−b3=(x−b)(x2+bx+b2)x and b are numbers.
Limit of a reciprocal power · Limits at infinitylimx→∞​xn1​=0n is a positive number.
Equal degrees · Limits at infinitylimx→∞​bxn+…axn+…​=ba​a and b are the leading coefficients of the numerator and denominator, and b=0.
Continuity at a · Continuitylimx→a​f(x)=f(a)It requires f(a) to be defined and the limit to exist.
Definition of the derivative · Tangents and instantaneous velocityf′(a)=limh→0​hf(a+h)−f(a)​f′(a) is the tangent slope at x=a, and h is a small amount going to zero.
Instantaneous velocity · Tangents and instantaneous velocityv(t)=s′(t)s is the position in metres, t the time in seconds, v the velocity in m/s.
Tangent line · Tangents and instantaneous velocityy−f(a)=f′(a)(x−a)A line through the point (a, f(a)) with slope f′(a).
Constant and linear function · Differentiation rules(k)′=0,(ax+b)′=ak, a and b are constants.
Power rule · Differentiation rules(xn)′=nxn−1n is a constant; for example (x4)′=4x3.
Sum and constant multiple · Differentiation rules(af+bg)′=af′+bg′a and b are constants, f and g are functions.
Product rule · Differentiation rules(f⋅g)′=f′⋅g+f⋅g′f and g are functions of x.
Chain rule · Differentiation rules((g(x))n)′=n(g(x))n−1⋅g′(x)g(x) is the inside expression and n the outside exponent.
Quotient rule · Differentiation rules(gf​)′=g2f′⋅g−f⋅g′​f and g are functions of x, and g=0.
Sign of the derivative · Increasing, decreasing and extreme valuesf′(x)>0⇒ increasingIf f′(x)<0 the function is decreasing on that interval.
Critical point · Increasing, decreasing and extreme valuesf′(x)=0Solving this equation gives the values of x that may give a minimum or maximum.

Integration

Definition of an antiderivative · AntiderivativesF′(x)=f(x)F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x). All antiderivatives are F(x)+C where C is a constant.
Power rule · Indefinite integrals and the power rule∫xndx=n+1xn+1​+Cwhere n=−1 and C is the constant of integration.
Integral of a constant · Indefinite integrals and the power rule∫kdx=kx+Ck is a constant.
Sum and constant multiple · Indefinite integrals and the power rule∫(kf(x)±g(x))dx=k∫f(x)dx±∫g(x)dxIntegrate each term separately and take out the constant multiplier.
Approximate area · Approximating area with rectanglesarea≈width×(sum of heights)width = number of rectanglesinterval length​, and each height is the function value at the chosen endpoint.
Fundamental Theorem · Definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem∫ab​f(x)dx=F(b)−F(a)F(x) is any antiderivative of f(x).
Derivative of an integral · Definite integrals and the Fundamental Theoremdxd​∫ax​f(t)dt=f(x)The derivative of an integral whose upper limit is x is the integrand itself with x in place of t.
Total change · Definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem∫ab​f′(x)dx=f(b)−f(a)The integral of the derivative gives the difference of the function values at the limits.
Swapping limits · Definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem∫ba​f(x)dx=−∫ab​f(x)dxSwapping the limits changes the sign.
Splitting · Definite integrals and the Fundamental Theorem∫ac​f(x)dx=∫ab​f(x)dx+∫bc​f(x)dxb is a point between a and c.
Area under a curve · Area under a curveA=∫ab​∣f(x)∣dxSplit the interval at the zeros, compute each part, take its absolute value and add.
Area between two curves · Area between two curvesA=∫ab​(f(x)−g(x))dxf(x)≥g(x) on the interval from a to b, and a and b are the intersection points.
Displacement · Distance and speed by integrationdisplacement=∫t1​t2​​v(t)dtVelocity in metres per second and time in seconds give displacement in metres.
Total distance · Distance and speed by integrationdistance=∫t1​t2​​∣v(t)∣dtIt equals the displacement if the velocity never changes sign.

Ratios, Percentages, Rates and Linear Models

Simplifying a ratio · Ratio and Proportionx:y=(x÷n):(y÷n)x and y are the terms of the ratio and n divides both (usually the greatest common factor).
Proportion · Ratio and Proportionyx​=wz​Two equal ratios.
Cross-multiplication · Ratio and Proportionx×w=y×zThe product of the extremes equals the product of the means.
Value of one part · Ratio and Proportionpart=sum of the partsquantity​Multiply by the number of parts each side has to get its share.
Inverse proportion · Ratio and Proportionx×y=constantExample: workers × days = total work, which is constant.
Part of a quantity · Percentagespart=100percent​×wholeThe percent is the number (such as 20); the whole is the original quantity.
The percent · Percentagespercent=wholepart​×100%Part and whole in the same unit.
Percent change · Percentagespercent change=originalchange​×100%The change is the difference between the new and the original value.
New value · Percentagesnew=original×(1±100percent​)Use + for an increase and − for a decrease.
Increase multiplier · Discounts and Successive Percent Changesmultiplier=1+100percent​A 20% rise has multiplier 1.2.
Decrease and discount multiplier · Discounts and Successive Percent Changesmultiplier=1−100percent​A 25% discount has multiplier 0.75.
Two successive changes · Discounts and Successive Percent Changesfinal=original×first multiplier×second multiplierThen total percent change = (final − original) ÷ original.
Whole from the part · Reverse Percentages and Finding the Wholewhole=percentpart​Write the percent as a decimal: 20% becomes 0.2.
Original value · Reverse Percentages and Finding the Wholeoriginal=multipliernew​The multiplier is 1.2 for a 20% rise and 0.75 for a 25% discount.
Speed · Rates and Speedspeed=timedistance​Distance in km and time in hours give speed in km/h.
Distance · Rates and Speeddistance=speed×timeUsed when speed and time are known.
Time · Rates and Speedtime=speeddistance​Comes out in hours if the speed is in km/h.
Average speed · Rates and Speedaverage speed=total timetotal distance​Usually different from the average of the two numbers.
Linear model · Linear Modelsy=mx+bx is the input, y the output, m the rate of change per unit, b the starting value.
Rate from two points · Linear Modelsm=x2​−x1​y2​−y1​​The points are (x1​,y1​) and (x2​,y2​).
Finding the input · Linear Modelsx=my−b​Subtract the starting value from the output, then divide by the rate.
